messages.subject: CANOPY (MDA-MB-231 example input)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jiang,

I hope you are doing good. My question is regarding the CANOPY input. Followed your protocol for MDA-MB-231 example, i.e., Called variants using UnifiedGenotyper, annotated them using annovar and kept those variants which were not called in 1000 Genomes Project, didn't reside in segmental duplication regions, in exonic baits and were deleterious by scoring matrices.. I am left with 216  variants associated with different genes.

Would you tell me how did you come up with the variants associated with 4 genes only. Which criterion did you use to select those variants?

Furthermore, two of the genes pinpointed in your study (i.e., BRAF and KRAS) are associated with dbSNP id. Don't we filter out those variants which have dbSNP ID, because they are usually thought to be germline mutations.  Or I am missing on some concept?

Looking forward to hear from you.

Best wishes,

AISHA

From: Jiang, Yuchao <yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu>
Sent: Monday, August 7, 2017 8:02 PM
To: Aisha Yousaf
Cc: canopy_p...@googlegroups.com
Subject: RE: CANOPY

Hi Aisha,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy. To detect somatic point mutations from tumor sequencing files is important and non-trivial however that is not the focus and contribution by Canopy. There are many methods developed for calling point mutations, for example, GATK, Mutect, Mutect2, VarScan2, etc. For our case, we don’t have a matched normal or normal to detect somatic mutations and thus we adopted the GATK UnifiedGenotyper, followed by stringent QC procedures to make sure that the variants called are truly somatic. The bash script for GATK we put on Canopy’s website is just for reference and is not maintained by us (but rather the GATK group in Broad). With this said, I will try to answer your questions.

1.       We use joint calling.

2.       We didn’t adopt VQSR but use Annovar to annotate all the variants and adopt stringent QC procedures (e.g., they aren’t called in the 1000 Genomes Project, they don’t reside in segmental duplication regions, and they are categorized as deleterious by scoring metrics such as CADD etc.).

Hope that this is of help to you.

Yuchao

From: Aisha Yousaf [mailto:aisha...@live.com]
Sent: Monday, August 7, 2017 4:59 AM
To: Jiang, Yuchao <yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu>
Subject: CANOPY

Hi Jiang,

I hope you are doing well.  I am interested to perform the analysis on MDA-MB-231 as you did in your article using CANOPY. Previously, I asked you for exome targets. Thank you for providing the targets. Until now, I have called variants using Unified Genotyper (based on the code you provided on GitHub). However, I have few questions regarding  MDA-MB-231 variant calling and filtration. Due to them, I am unable to move ahead.

As per MDA-MB-231 example in CANOPY paper,

 Should I call variants on all samples together and get a single VCF output or individually on each samples and then merge them?
How did you filter the variants in that particular case? According to GATK , we cannot apply VQSR (Variant Quality Score Recalibration) to less than 30 exomes.

Thanks for your time and any possible help in this regard.

Best wishes,

AISHA

How to call somatic point mutations (in this case without normal control) is beyond the scope of Canopy. This is an active research area and I would recommend you refer to sources and information from Mutect, Mutect2, VarScan2, etc. Just for your information, we annotate all variants and use the CADD scores etc. to determine the functional consequences of all variants. The two mutations in BRAF and KRAS in MDA-MB-231 have been previously reported. Please see the paper we cross compare in our PNAS paper.

Hope this helps,
Yuchao

messages.subject: RE: falconx
messages.body_plain:
Yes that is correct. You should refer to below:

Tumor phylogeny analysis by WES
Experimental design: WES/WGS of multiple spatially or temporally separated tumor samples with matched normal, greater than 20 normal controls (no need to be matched)
Script: Profiling somatic point mutations <https://github.com/yuchaojiang/MARATHON/blob/master/script/somatic_SNV.sh>, CODEX2 --> FALCON-X <https://github.com/yuchaojiang/MARATHON/blob/master/script/CODEX2_FALCONX.R>, Canopy <https://github.com/yuchaojiang/MARATHON/blob/master/script/Canopy.R>
More details: CODEX2 <https://github.com/yuchaojiang/CODEX2>, FALCON-X <https://cran.r-project.org/package=falconx>, Canopy <https://github.com/yuchaojiang/Canopy>

From: Patidar, Rajesh (NIH/NCI) [C] [mailto:rajesh....@nih.gov]
Sent: Wednesday, November 8, 2017 9:51 AM
To: Jiang, Yuchao <yuc...@email.unc.edu>; Hao Chen <hxc...@ucdavis.edu>
Subject: RE: falconx

Hi Yuchao,

Thanks for the email. Could you please let me know if my following understanding is correct or not?

Steps:

Run https://github.com/yuchaojiang/MARATHON/blob/master/script/CODEX2.R ==> I ran this successfully

Run  https://github.com/yuchaojiang/MARATHON/blob/master/script/CODEX2_FALCONX.R

Run https://github.com/yuchaojiang/MARATHON/blob/master/script/Canopy.R

Where does a test sample fit in this procedure? Sorry but for different scripts different example data is used which is making me a bit confusing as I am not an R expert yet.

Thanks,

Rajesh

From: Jiang, Yuchao [mailto:yuc...@email.unc.edu]
Sent: Wednesday, November 8, 2017 9:33 AM
To: Patidar, Rajesh (NIH/NCI) [C] <rajesh....@nih.gov>; Hao Chen <hxc...@ucdavis.edu>
Subject: RE: falconx

Hi Rajesh,

We tried as much as we can to give a unified framework/script. However, a lot of the upstream processing are different across different research groups – this includes different data quality (and thus different QC should be adopted) and even different vcf format (depending on which caller you need). With this said, we also recommend that you run the demo code with the demo dataset yourself first before applying CODEX2/FALCON-X/Canopy to your dataset. The change from the demo to your dataset should not be on the major functions of these software but mostly, if not all, on the pre-processing step and post-calling quality control/filtering.

Hope this helps! If we have more bandwidth to further integrate the codes, we will let you know.

Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: Integrative pipeline for profiling DNA copy,number and inferring tumor phylogeny and Canopy
messages.subject_clean: Integrative pipeline for profiling DNA copy,number and inferring tumor phylogeny and Canopy
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kay,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy. Do you have normal controls for the tumor samples? If so, you can use FALCON to call allele-specific copy numbers. The point mutations are stored in your VCFs. However, you should adopt stringent QC and functional annotations on these mutations. Then the ASCNs and point mutations can be fed into Canopy to infer tumor phylogeny. CODEX is for total copy number analysis and doesn’t apply to the goal you mentioned in your email.

Hope this is helpful,
Yuchao

> Hi Nancy,
>
> I hope you are doing good. I read your article entitled "Assessing intra-tumor heterogeneity and tracking longitudinal and spatial clonal evolution by next-generation sequencing". I am interested in applying that method ('CANOPY') to reproduce the results for MDA-MB-231 example. I followed the entire protocol for SNV calling but I am having trouble in CNA profiling for that particular example, having tumor-only samples (no normal available.) I read the supplementary also, but the things are not quite clear to me.
>
> I have some questions regarding that:
>
> How did you calculated BAF on SCP samples and on which file format? I couldn't find any standardized method for calculating BAF.

BAF stands for B allele frequency at heterozygous loci, which is used to infer copy number together with depth ratio. BAF can be calculated from VCF files. VCF can be obtained from SNP callers, such as GATK.

> How did you apply HMM on the input BAFs. Does it involve any R package or software?

We implement our own HMM to infer copy number states from BAFs. The emission and transition probabilities are in the supplementary tables. After segmentation using BAFs, the actual copy numbers are inferred/manually adjusted based on depth of coverage ratios. This whole analysis arose because we don’t have paired normal samples to directly infer allele-specific copy numbers.

>
> In case of SNVs, after following the entire filtering procedure, as mentioned in your article,  I am left with 216 variants associated with 4 different genes. How did you come up with the variants associated with 4 genes only. Which process did you apply?

I’ve replied to this before — you need to functionally annotate these mutations and we select for those that are highly deleterious.

>
> Furthermore, two of the genes pinpointed in your study (i.e., BRAF and KRAS) are associated with dbSNP id. Don't we filter out those variants which have dbSNP ID, because they are usually thought to be germline mutations. Or I am missing on some concept?

These mutations are highly deleterious. Furthermore and more importantly, they have been validated by deep sequencing by a different study which we cited, using deep sequencing. See Jacob et al. reference 37.

>
> I will be really grateful to your response in this regard. I am stuck on this problem from quite sometime.
>
> Looking forward to hear from you soon.
>
> Best wishes,
> AISHA
